statement: For a [compact Hausdorff space](c:compact-hausdorff-space) $X$ and $n \ge 1$, the map $x_1+\dots+x_n \mapsto (f \mapsto \sum_i f(x_i))$ is a bijection from the [symmetric product](c:symmetric-product) $SP^n(X)$ onto the set of continuous linear $\varphi\colon C(X)\to\mathbb{C}$ with $\varphi(1)=n$ that satisfy the Frobenius $n$-homomorphism identity.

hypotheses.text: The space $X$ is a [compact Hausdorff space](c:compact-hausdorff-space).
The integer $n$ is at least $1$.

conclusion: Every such $\varphi$ is a sum of $n$ point evaluations, unique up to order, and every such sum satisfies the identity.

proofs.name: Frobenius identity and finite support
proofs.slogan: Check that point-evaluation sums satisfy the identity, then show that a continuous solution is supported on at most $n$ points with integer weights.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for $n\ge1$; the case $n=1$ is the Gelfand-Kolmogorov embedding. The proof is an outline and the support step rests on the cited paper.

roles.why: Compactness and the Hausdorff property give Urysohn functions and a Riesz measure for $\varphi$.
The integer $n$ bounds the number of points and the size of the antisymmetrization.

steps.slogan: Check that a sum of $n$ point evaluations satisfies the Frobenius identity.
steps.detail: Write $\varphi=\operatorname{tr}\circ\rho$ with $\rho(f)=\operatorname{diag}(f(x_1),\dots,f(x_n))$, an algebra map into $M_n(\mathbb{C})$. The signed sum over $S_{n+1}$ of products of traces is the trace of an antisymmetrization on $\Lambda^{n+1}\mathbb{C}^n=0$, so it vanishes. Also $\varphi(1)=n$.

steps.slogan: Show that distinct multisets of points give distinct functionals.
steps.detail: Point evaluations at distinct points are linearly independent, since Urysohn's lemma gives functions that separate finitely many points. So the multiset is recovered from the functional, and the map is injective.

steps.slogan: Show that a continuous solution has finite support of at most $n$ points.
steps.detail: By the Riesz representation theorem $\varphi$ is a measure. The identity applied to functions with pairwise disjoint supports forces the support to be finite with at most $n$ points; this is the step of the cited paper.

steps.slogan: Show that the weights are positive integers with sum $n$.
steps.detail: On a small neighborhood of one support point, the identity reduces to the same identity for the local weight. This forces the weight to be an integer, and $\varphi(1)=n$ fixes the sum.

steps.slogan: Conclude that the map is a bijection onto the solution set.
steps.detail: Every solution is a sum of $n$ evaluations with multiplicity, so the map is onto. Step 1 shows the image consists of solutions, and step 2 gives injectivity.

concepts.c:compact-hausdorff-space: Compact Hausdorff spaces support Urysohn functions and Riesz measures.
concepts.c:symmetric-product: Its points are the multisets of $n$ points that index the functionals.

source.ref: V. M. Buchstaber and E. G. Rees, The Gelfand map and symmetric products, Selecta Mathematica (N.S.) 8 (2002), 523-535
source.note: The paper proves the characterization of the image of the symmetric power. Step 1 is a standard trace computation.

statement: Let $\mathcal I$ be a regular [exterior differential system](c:exterior-differential-system) on a smooth manifold $M$. After finitely many prolongations the system is [involutive](c:involutive-system), or it has no integral elements and is impossible.

hypotheses.text: $\mathcal I$ is an [exterior differential system](c:exterior-differential-system) on a manifold $M$.
Every prolongation of $\mathcal I$ is regular: the integral elements form a smooth bundle of constant rank.

conclusion: Some prolongation $\mathcal I^{(k)}$ is involutive or has an empty set of integral elements.

proofs.name: Kuranishi's outline
proofs.slogan: Prolong the system, observe that the symbol stabilizes by a Noetherian argument, and read involutivity from the Cartan test.
proofs.scope: The smooth regular case, as an outline; the algebraic stabilization is the cited work of Kuranishi. Other versions, such as the analytic case, are not covered.

roles.why: The system supplies the integral elements that the prolongation tower is built from.
Regularity keeps each prolongation a smooth system with constant-rank symbol.

steps.slogan: Build the prolongation tower of integral elements.
steps.detail: The integral elements of $\mathcal I$ form a bundle over $M$. Its contact system defines the first prolongation, and repeating this gives $\mathcal I^{(k)}$ for all $k$, or an empty stage.

steps.slogan: Attach to each prolongation its symbol and Cartan characters.
steps.detail: At each stage the tableau of the system is a graded module over a polynomial ring in $n$ variables. Its Cartan characters bound the dimension of integral elements, and equality is the Cartan test.

steps.slogan: Show that the symbol module stabilizes after finitely many prolongations.
steps.detail: The relevant Spencer-type cohomology of the module is finitely generated over a Noetherian ring, so it vanishes beyond some order. After that order the prolongation's symbol is the prolongation of the previous one.

steps.slogan: Apply the Cartan test beyond the stabilization order.
steps.detail: Past that order, the dimensions of integral elements match the character bound, so the Cartan test holds at every point of the stage. A stage with no integral elements is the impossible case.

steps.slogan: Conclude that some prolongation is involutive or empty.
steps.detail: Either the tower has an empty stage, or at the stabilization order the test of step 4 shows the stage is involutive.

concepts.c:exterior-differential-system: It is the object whose prolongations are studied.
concepts.c:involutive-system: Involutivity is the outcome the Cartan test certifies.

source.ref: M. Kuranishi, On E. Cartan's prolongation theorem of exterior differential systems, American Journal of Mathematics 79 (1957), 1-47
source.note: Kuranishi proves the finiteness of the prolongation process; Bryant, Chern, Gardner, Goldschmidt and Griffiths, Exterior Differential Systems (MSRI Publications 18, Springer 1991) give a textbook account.

statement: Let $\mathcal C,\mathcal D$ be categories, $F$ an assignment of an object $Fc$ to each object $c$, and $P(f,g)$ a relation between $f\colon c\to c'$ and $g\colon Fc\to Fc'$. If $P$ respects identities and composition and each $f$ has exactly one $g$ with $P(f,g)$, then $F$ extends uniquely to a [functor](c:functor) with $P(f,Ff)$.

hypotheses.text: The object assignment $F$ and the relation $P$ are given on [categories](c:functor) $\mathcal C,\mathcal D$.
$P(1_c, 1_{Fc})$ holds for every object $c$.
$P(f,g)$ and $P(f',g')$ imply $P(f'f, g'g)$.
Each morphism $f$ has exactly one $g$ with $P(f,g)$.

conclusion: There is exactly one functor $F\colon \mathcal C\to\mathcal D$ that agrees with the given objects and has $P(f,Ff)$ for every $f$.

proofs.name: Uniqueness of the witness
proofs.slogan: Define the action on morphisms as the unique witness, then let uniqueness force identities and composites.
proofs.scope: This is the unique-existence form of the principle for ordinary categories. Other forms, such as the adjoint-functor and Yoneda forms, and the higher-categorical versions are not covered.

roles.why: The assignment on objects and the relation $P$ are the input to the construction.
Together with uniqueness, it gives $F(1_c)=1_{Fc}$.
Together with uniqueness, it gives $F(f'f)=Ff'\circ Ff$.
It makes $Ff$ well defined and decides every equality in the proof.

steps.slogan: Define $Ff$ as the unique $g$ with $P(f,g)$.
steps.detail: For each $f\colon c\to c'$ the hypothesis gives exactly one $g\colon Fc\to Fc'$ with $P(f,g)$. Set $Ff=g$. This defines $F$ on morphisms with the correct source and target.

steps.slogan: Show that $F$ preserves identities.
steps.detail: Both $1_{Fc}$ and $F(1_c)$ satisfy $P(1_c,-)$ by the first hypothesis and the definition. Uniqueness gives $F(1_c)=1_{Fc}$.

steps.slogan: Show that $F$ preserves composition.
steps.detail: For composable $f,f'$, the pairs $(f,Ff)$ and $(f',Ff')$ satisfy $P$, so $P(f'f, Ff'\circ Ff)$ holds. Also $P(f'f,F(f'f))$ holds by definition. Uniqueness gives $F(f'f)=Ff'\circ Ff$.

steps.slogan: Show that any functor with the same objects and property $P$ equals $F$.
steps.detail: Let $G$ be a functor with $Gc=Fc$ and $P(f,Gf)$ for all $f$. Then $Gf$ is a witness for $f$, so $Gf=Ff$ by uniqueness. Hence $G=F$, and $F$ is the only such functor.

concepts.c:functor: The result is a functor, so identities and composition must be preserved.

source.note: A direct proof of the unique-existence form; compare the nLab entry on functor comprehension and Mac Lane, Categories for the Working Mathematician, chapter IV (construction of adjoints from universal arrows).

statement: Let $\mathcal A$ be a finite sequence of integers, $S(\mathcal A,\mathcal P,z)$ its [sifted](c:sieve) count, and suppose $|\mathcal A_d|=\frac{\omega(d)}{d}X+R_d$ with $\omega$ of linear sieve dimension. Then for $2\le z\le D$, $S\le XV(z)\{F(s)+E\}+\sum_{d<D,\,d\mid P(z)}3^{\nu(d)}|R_d|$ with $s=\log D/\log z$, $F(s)=2e^{\gamma}/s$ for $0<s\le 3$, and $E\to0$ as $D\to\infty$.

hypotheses.text: For [squarefree](c:squarefree-integer) $d\mid P(z)$, $|\mathcal A_d|=\frac{\omega(d)}{d}X+R_d$ with $\omega$ multiplicative.
The function $\omega$ has sieve dimension $1$: $0\le\omega(p)/p\le 1-1/A$ and $\sum_{w\le p<z}\omega(p)\log p/p\le\log(z/w)+A$.
The level $D$ and the sifting limit $z$ satisfy $2\le z\le D$.

conclusion: The sifted count has the stated upper bound, with main term $XV(z)F(s)$ and a remainder sum over $d<D$.

proofs.name: Improved Selberg sieve
proofs.slogan: Bound the sifted count by Selberg's quadratic form, diagonalize it, and choose the weights of Jurkat and Richert to get the optimal main term.
proofs.scope: An outline of the published proof for sieve dimension $1$; the explicit error term $E$ and the weight optimization rest on the cited paper.

roles.why: The density formula turns the quadratic form into a main term plus remainders $R_d$.
The dimension condition controls the main term and the choice of weights.
The level $D$ limits the support of the weights and the remainder range.

steps.slogan: Majorize the sifting indicator by a square of weights supported below $D$.
steps.detail: Choose real $\lambda_d$ with $\lambda_1=1$, supported on $d\mid P(z)$, $d<\sqrt D$. Then $\mathbf 1_{(n,P(z))=1}\le(\sum_{d\mid n}\lambda_d)^2$, so $S$ is at most the sum of this square over $\mathcal A$.

steps.slogan: Expand the square and insert the density formula.
steps.detail: The expansion gives $X\sum_{d,e}\lambda_d\lambda_e\,\omega([d,e])/[d,e]$ plus a remainder $\sum|\lambda_d\lambda_e||R_{[d,e]}|$. The first part is a quadratic form in the weights.

steps.slogan: Diagonalize the quadratic form by Selberg's change of variables.
steps.detail: Substituting new variables $y_l$ for the weights makes the form a sum of squares, $\sum_l g(l)\,y_l^2$ with $g$ multiplicative. The condition $\lambda_1=1$ becomes one linear constraint on the $y_l$.

steps.slogan: Choose the weights of Jurkat and Richert to minimize the main term.
steps.detail: Jurkat and Richert modify Selberg's optimal choice so that the weights satisfy $|\lambda_d|\le1$. They evaluate the minimum using the dimension condition and obtain $XV(z)\{F(s)+E\}$ with $F(s)=2e^{\gamma}/s$ in the range $0<s\le3$.

steps.slogan: Bound the remainder by the sum over $d<D$.
steps.detail: Since $|\lambda_d|\le1$ and each $d<D$ appears as $[d_1,d_2]$ in at most $3^{\nu(d)}$ ways, the remainder is at most $\sum_{d<D,\,d\mid P(z)}3^{\nu(d)}|R_d|$.

concepts.c:sieve: The theorem bounds the count of integers that survive a sieve.
concepts.c:squarefree-integer: Sieve moduli $d$ are squarefree products of primes.

source.ref: W. B. Jurkat and H.-E. Richert, An improvement of Selberg's sieve method I, Acta Arithmetica 11 (1965), 217-240
source.note: The paper proves the bound for sieve dimension 1; H. Halberstam and H.-E. Richert, Sieve Methods (Academic Press, 1974) give the textbook version used for Chen's theorem.

statement: The Kanamori-McAloon principle holds: for all $n,k$ there is $m$ such that every [regressive](c:regressive-function) colouring $f$ of the $n$-subsets of $\{1,\dots,m\}$ has a relatively large min-homogeneous set $H$ with $|H|\ge k$. If [Peano arithmetic](c:peano-arithmetic) is consistent, it does not prove this principle.

hypotheses.text: [Peano arithmetic](c:peano-arithmetic) is consistent.

conclusion: The principle is true, yet not provable in Peano arithmetic.

proofs.name: Truth by compactness, unprovability by Paris-Harrington
proofs.slogan: Prove the principle from the infinite regressive Ramsey theorem, then show that it implies the Paris-Harrington principle, which Peano arithmetic cannot prove.
proofs.scope: An outline; the exact form of the principle (the largeness condition) and the reduction follow the cited paper. The truth part is a proof in stronger theories than Peano arithmetic.

roles.why: Consistency of Peano arithmetic is what makes unprovability a real statement.

steps.slogan: Prove the infinite regressive Ramsey theorem.
steps.detail: A regressive colouring of $[\mathbb N]^n$ has an infinite min-homogeneous set. This follows by induction on $n$ from Ramsey's theorem applied to the canonical partition of $n$-subsets.

steps.slogan: Pass to the finite principle by compactness.
steps.detail: If the finite principle failed for some $n,k$, König's lemma would assemble counterexamples for every $m$ into a regressive colouring of $[\mathbb N]^n$ with no min-homogeneous set of size $k$, against step 1.

steps.slogan: Show that the principle implies the Paris-Harrington principle over Peano arithmetic.
steps.detail: Kanamori and McAloon code a Paris-Harrington colouring into a regressive one. A min-homogeneous set of the required size then gives a homogeneous set of the Paris-Harrington kind.

steps.slogan: Use the unprovability of the Paris-Harrington principle in Peano arithmetic.
steps.detail: Paris and Harrington showed that their principle is true but not provable in Peano arithmetic, if that theory is consistent. So the principle of step 3 cannot be provable either.

steps.slogan: Combine truth and unprovability.
steps.detail: Step 2 shows the principle is true in the standard model. Steps 3 and 4 show Peano arithmetic does not prove it.

concepts.c:regressive-function: Regressive colourings are the objects of the principle.
concepts.c:peano-arithmetic: The theory in which the principle is unprovable.

source.ref: A. Kanamori and K. McAloon, On Goedel incompleteness and finite combinatorics, Annals of Pure and Applied Logic 33 (1987), 23-41
source.note: The paper states the regressive Ramsey principle and proves its independence from Peano arithmetic.

statement: For [almost every](c:almost-everywhere) $x\in(0,1)$, let $m(n)$ be the number of [continued fraction](c:continued-fraction) partial quotients of $x$ fixed by its first $n$ decimal digits. Then $m(n)/n\to \dfrac{6\ln 2\,\ln 10}{\pi^2}\approx 0.97027$.

hypotheses.text: The number $x$ lies outside a fixed set of [Lebesgue measure](c:lebesgue-measure) zero.

conclusion: The limit of $m(n)/n$ exists and equals $6\ln2\ln10/\pi^2$.

proofs.name: Cylinder lengths and Borel-Cantelli
proofs.slogan: Compare the length $10^{-n}$ of the decimal interval with the length of the continued fraction cylinder, using Levy's constant and a Borel-Cantelli bound on boundary distance.
proofs.scope: For almost every $x$; the null set contains the rationals and the points where the limits below fail. Here $m(n)$ is the largest $m$ with the decimal interval of $x$ inside the rank-$m$ cylinder of $x$.

roles.why: Excluding a null set lets the ergodic theorem and Borel-Cantelli apply to the point $x$.

steps.slogan: Find the growth rate of the denominators $q_m$ by the ergodic theorem.
steps.detail: The Gauss map preserves the measure $dx/((1+x)\ln2)$ and is [ergodic](c:ergodic). Since $x\,Tx\cdots T^{m-1}x\asymp 1/q_m$, Birkhoff's theorem gives $\frac1m\ln q_m\to\pi^2/(12\ln2)$ almost everywhere.

steps.slogan: Compute the length of the rank-$m$ cylinder of $x$.
steps.detail: The cylinder is an interval of length $1/(q_m(q_m+q_{m-1}))$, and $q_{m-1}\le q_m$. With step 1, $\frac1m\ln|C_m(x)|\to-\pi^2/(6\ln2)$.

steps.slogan: Show by Borel-Cantelli that $x$ lies far from its cylinder ends.
steps.detail: Fix $\varepsilon>0$. The points of rank-$m$ cylinders within $e^{-\varepsilon m}|C|$ of an end have total measure at most $2e^{-\varepsilon m}$. This is summable, so almost every $x$ has distance at least $e^{-\varepsilon m}|C_m(x)|$ to the ends for large $m$.

steps.slogan: Bound $m(n)$ above and below by cylinder lengths.
steps.detail: If the decimal interval lies in $C_m(x)$, then $10^{-n}\le|C_m(x)|$. If $10^{-n}<e^{-\varepsilon m}|C_m(x)|$, then the interval, which contains $x$, stays inside $C_m(x)$ by step 3.

steps.slogan: Take logarithms and let $\varepsilon$ tend to zero.
steps.detail: By steps 2 and 4, $m(n)\,\pi^2/(6\ln2)=n\ln10\,(1+o(1))+O(\varepsilon m)$. Letting $\varepsilon\to0$ gives $m(n)/n\to 6\ln2\ln10/\pi^2$.

concepts.c:almost-everywhere: The statement holds outside a null set of starting points.
concepts.c:continued-fraction: The partial quotients and their cylinders are the objects counted.
concepts.c:lebesgue-measure: Null sets and cylinder lengths are measured by Lebesgue measure.
concepts.c:ergodic: Ergodicity of the Gauss map gives the constant for $q_m$.

source.note: The argument of Lochs (1964), as in Khinchin, Continued Fractions, and Bosma, Jager and Wiedijk (1983); it uses Levy's theorem.

statement: Let $\pi$ be the [prime counting function](c:prime-counting-function) and $\lambda>1$. Then $\dfrac{\pi(x+(\log x)^\lambda)-\pi(x)}{(\log x)^{\lambda-1}}$ has no limit as $x\to\infty$: its limit superior exceeds $1$ and its limit inferior is below $1$.

hypotheses.text: The exponent $\lambda$ is a real number greater than $1$.

conclusion: The normalized count of primes in $(x,x+(\log x)^\lambda]$ oscillates around $1$, against the [Cramer model](c:cramer-model).

proofs.name: Maier's matrix method
proofs.slogan: Sieve the short windows $[Qm+1,Qm+y]$ by the small primes in $Q$, then compare the average count with the Buchstab function.
proofs.scope: Outline of Maier's proof for fixed $\lambda>1$; the equidistribution of primes in progressions modulo $Q$ rests on the cited paper.

roles.why: The window length $y=(\log x)^\lambda$ is much larger than $\log y$ steps of the sieve, so the sieve is nontrivial.

steps.slogan: Arrange the integers up to $x$ in windows of length $y=(\log x)^\lambda$ modulo $Q$.
steps.detail: Let $Q$ be the product of the primes up to $z=y^{1/u}$ for a fixed $u$. Row $m$ is the window $Qm+1,\dots,Qm+y$, and column $j$ holds $Qm+j$.

steps.slogan: Count the columns that can hold primes.
steps.detail: A column with $\gcd(j,Q)>1$ holds no prime. The number of admissible $j\le y$ is $(\omega(u)+o(1))\,y/\log z$, where $\omega$ is the Buchstab function.

steps.slogan: Distribute the primes over the admissible columns by equidistribution.
steps.detail: Each admissible column receives about $\pi(x)/\varphi(Q)$ primes, because primes are equidistributed in progressions modulo $Q$ for a suitable choice of $z$. This is the deep input of the cited paper, which handles possible exceptional zeros.

steps.slogan: Compute the average number of primes per window.
steps.detail: By Mertens' theorem $Q/\varphi(Q)\sim e^{\gamma}\log z$. So the average is $(e^{\gamma}\omega(u)+o(1))\,y/\log x$.

steps.slogan: Pick $u$ where $e^{\gamma}\omega(u)$ is above $1$ and where it is below $1$.
steps.detail: The function $\omega(u)-e^{-\gamma}$ changes sign infinitely often. A window above the average gives $\limsup>1$, and a window below the average, from another $u$, gives $\liminf<1$.

concepts.c:prime-counting-function: The ratio counts primes in a short window.
concepts.c:cramer-model: The theorem shows that the model's prediction of a limit is false.

source.ref: H. Maier, Primes in short intervals, Michigan Mathematical Journal 32 (1985), 221-225
source.note: Maier's paper introduces the matrix method and proves the theorem.

statement: Let $T$ be a finitely splitting rooted [tree](c:rooted-tree) of height $\omega$ without terminal nodes, $n\ge1$, and colour the [strong subtrees](c:strong-subtree) of $T$ of height $n$ with finitely many colours. Then some strong subtree $S\subseteq T$ of height $\omega$ has all its height-$n$ strong subtrees of one colour.

hypotheses.text: The tree $T$ is a finitely splitting [rooted tree](c:rooted-tree) of height $\omega$ with no terminal nodes.
The height-$n$ [strong subtrees](c:strong-subtree) of $T$ are coloured with finitely many colours.

conclusion: There is a strong subtree of height $\omega$ whose height-$n$ strong subtrees are monochromatic.

proofs.name: From the Halpern-Lauchli theorem
proofs.slogan: Prove the case of one level by the Halpern-Lauchli theorem, then raise the height by a fusion argument over finite strong subtrees.
proofs.scope: An outline of Milliken's proof for all $n$; the Halpern-Lauchli step and the fusion details rest on the cited work. The tree $T$ is assumed to have no terminal nodes so that strong subtrees of height $\omega$ exist.

roles.why: Finite splitting makes each level finite, so the strong-subtree structure and fusion are available.
The finite colouring is what the pigeonhole steps of Halpern-Lauchli refine.

steps.slogan: State the strong-subtree form of the Halpern-Lauchli theorem.
steps.detail: For finitely many finitely splitting trees and a finite colouring of their level products, there are a strong subtree level set and a common level sequence on which the colour is constant. This is the engine of the proof.

steps.slogan: Treat height $n=1$ by applying the theorem to one tree.
steps.detail: For $n=1$ a strong subtree of height $1$ is a node. Halpern-Lauchli for one tree gives a strong subtree of height $\omega$ all of whose nodes have one colour.

steps.slogan: Raise the height from $n$ to $n+1$ using finite strong subtrees.
steps.detail: Fix a finite strong subtree $F$ of height $n$. Colour each extension of $F$ by one level by the colour of the resulting height-$(n+1)$ tree. Apply Halpern-Lauchli to the finitely many cones above the top of $F$.

steps.slogan: Fuse the choices into one strong subtree of height $\omega$.
steps.detail: Choose the levels of $S$ one at a time. At each stage thin the remaining tree by step 3 for every finite strong subtree built so far. The finitely many such subtrees make the thinning finite.

steps.slogan: Conclude that all height-$n$ strong subtrees of $S$ have one colour.
steps.detail: Every height-$n$ strong subtree of $S$ was handled at some stage of the fusion, and the thinning gave all of them the same colour.

concepts.c:rooted-tree: The theorem concerns a finitely splitting rooted tree of height $\omega$.
concepts.c:strong-subtree: Strong subtrees are the objects that are coloured and found.

source.ref: K. R. Milliken, A Ramsey theorem for trees, Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series A 26 (1979), 215-237
source.note: Milliken's paper; S. Todorcevic, Introduction to Ramsey Spaces (Annals of Mathematics Studies 174, Princeton University Press, 2010) gives a modern proof.

statement: Let $a_1,\dots,a_k$ be positive integers and colour $\mathbb N$ with finitely many colours. Then there is a strictly increasing sequence $(x_t)$ such that all sums $\sum_{i=1}^k a_i\sum_{t\in F_i}x_t$ with $F_1<\dots<F_k$ finite nonempty sets have one colour.

hypotheses.text: The numbers $a_1,\dots,a_k$ are positive integers.
The set $\mathbb N$ is coloured with finitely many colours.

conclusion: Some sequence $(x_t)$ gives a monochromatic Milliken-Taylor system $\{\sum_i a_i\sum_{t\in F_i}x_t : F_1<\dots<F_k\}$.

proofs.name: Idempotent ultrafilter
proofs.slogan: Take an idempotent ultrafilter $p$, form $a_1p+\dots+a_kp$, and build the sequence inside one of its members.
proofs.scope: All $k\ge1$ with positive coefficients. The case $k=1$ is Hindman's theorem; an outline whose sequence construction follows the cited book.

roles.why: Positive multipliers define the maps $y\mapsto a_iy$ that act on ultrafilters.
One colour class lies in the [ultrafilter](c:ultrafilter) $q$.

steps.slogan: Choose an [idempotent](c:idempotent) ultrafilter $p$ on $\mathbb N$.
steps.detail: The sum of ultrafilters is associative and right continuous on $\beta\mathbb N$. By the Ellis-Numakura lemma there is an idempotent $p=p+p$; each member of $p$ contains an IP set, as in Hindman's theorem.

steps.slogan: Form $q=a_1p+\dots+a_kp$ and pick the colour class $A\in q$.
steps.detail: Multiplication by $a_i$ is a homomorphism of $(\mathbb N,+)$, so each $a_ip$ is an ultrafilter. Their sum $q$ is an ultrafilter, so one of the finitely many colour classes $A$ belongs to $q$.

steps.slogan: Unfold the membership $A\in q$ into nested sets of $p$.
steps.detail: $A\in a_1p+q'$ means $\{y:-a_1y+A\in q'\}\in p$, where $q'=a_2p+\dots+a_kp$. Repeating, each stage gives a set of $p$ that describes which earlier sums allow a next sum in $A$.

steps.slogan: Choose $x_1<x_2<\dots$ so that finite sums stay in these sets.
steps.detail: At each stage take $x_t$ in the finite intersection of the required members of $p$, and in the set $B^*=\{x\in B:-x+B\in p\}$ that idempotence supplies. Then every finite sum of the $x_t$ remains in $B$.

steps.slogan: Check that every block sum lies in $A$.
steps.detail: For $F_1<\dots<F_k$ the sum $\sum a_i\sum_{t\in F_i}x_t$ falls in $A$ by the nested choices of step 4, so the system is monochromatic.

concepts.c:ultrafilter: A colour class belongs to the ultrafilter, so it carries the system.
concepts.c:idempotent: Idempotence $p=p+p$ lets sums of chosen elements stay in a member of $p$.

source.ref: N. Hindman and D. Strauss, Algebra in the Stone-Cech Compactification, 2nd edition, de Gruyter, 2012
source.note: The book gives the ultrafilter proof of the Milliken-Taylor theorem; the original results are K. Milliken, J. Combin. Theory Ser. A 18 (1975) and A. D. Taylor, J. Combin. Theory Ser. A 21 (1976).

statement: Let $\Omega$ be a smooth [convex](c:convex-curve) oval, the region bounded by a $C^\infty$ closed [convex curve](c:convex-curve) in the plane. The [area](c:area) $S(\ell)$ cut off by a secant line $\ell$ is not an [algebraic function](c:algebraic-function) of $\ell$.

hypotheses.text: The boundary of $\Omega$ is an infinitely differentiable closed [convex curve](c:convex-curve).

conclusion: No nonzero polynomial relation in the line coordinates and $S$ holds for all secants of $\Omega$.

proofs.name: Newton's spiral, after Arnold
proofs.slogan: Rotate a line about a boundary point, accumulate the swept area over many turns, and show that the resulting spiral meets a line infinitely often.
proofs.scope: The smooth oval; the step that passes from an algebraic area function to an algebraic spiral is the rigorous part of Arnold's treatment and rests on the cited paper.

roles.why: Smoothness and convexity make the chord length $c(\theta)$ and the area function well behaved.

steps.slogan: Rotate a line about a boundary point and differentiate the cut-off area.
steps.detail: Fix a point $O$ on the oval and let $\ell_\theta$ pass through $O$ at angle $\theta$. If $c(\theta)$ is the chord length, then $dS/d\theta=c(\theta)^2/2$.

steps.slogan: Let the line turn through many turns and accumulate the swept area.
steps.detail: Set $A(\theta)=\int c^2/2\,d\theta$, with $c=0$ for lines missing the oval. Then $A(\theta+2\pi)=A(\theta)+\operatorname{Area}(\Omega)$, so the point at distance $A(\theta)$ from $O$ on $\ell_\theta$ traces a spiral.

steps.slogan: Show that an algebraic area function makes the spiral algebraic.
steps.detail: On each turn $A(\theta)=S(\ell_\theta)+k\operatorname{Area}(\Omega)$. Arnold proves for smooth ovals that algebraicity of $S$ forces the spiral to lie on an algebraic curve.

steps.slogan: Count the intersections of the spiral with a line through $O$.
steps.detail: The line $\ell_{\theta_0}$ contains the spiral points for $\theta_0+k\pi$, with distances growing without bound. So the spiral meets this line in infinitely many points.

steps.slogan: Contradict Bezout's bound for algebraic curves.
steps.detail: An algebraic curve that does not contain the line $\ell_{\theta_0}$ meets it in finitely many points. The spiral does not contain this line, so the curve is not algebraic, and $S$ is not an algebraic function.

concepts.c:convex-curve: Convexity makes each secant cut off one well-defined region.
concepts.c:area: The area cut off by a secant is the function studied.
concepts.c:algebraic-function: Algebraicity of the area is the property refuted.

source.ref: V. I. Arnold and V. A. Vassiliev, Newton's Principia read 300 years later, Notices of the American Mathematical Society 36 (1989), 1148-1154
source.note: The paper explains Newton's Lemma XXVIII and makes his argument rigorous for infinitely differentiable ovals.

statement: Let the forward amplitudes of $\kappa_1\kappa_2$ and $\kappa_1\bar\kappa_2$ be related by crossing, obey the optical theorem and a once-subtracted [dispersion relation](c:dispersion-relation) for their odd combination, and let their [cross sections](c:cross-section) tend to finite limits with bounded real-to-imaginary ratio. Then the cross-section difference tends to $0$.

hypotheses.text: The forward amplitudes $F_{ab}(E)$ and $F_{a\bar b}(E)$ are boundary values of one [analytic function](c:analytic-function) with $F_{a\bar b}(E)=F_{ab}(-E)$.
The optical theorem holds: $\operatorname{Im}F=k\sigma$ for each process.
The odd combination satisfies a once-subtracted dispersion relation.
The cross sections $\sigma_{ab},\sigma_{a\bar b}$ tend to finite limits as $E\to\infty$.
The ratio $\operatorname{Re}F_-(E)/E$ stays bounded, where $F_-=F_{ab}-F_{a\bar b}$.

proofs.name: Dispersion relation for the odd amplitude
proofs.slogan: Assume that the difference tends to $d\ne0$, compute the real part of the odd amplitude from the dispersion relation, and contradict the bounded ratio.
proofs.scope: A mathematical derivation under the stated hypotheses; the principal-value integral of the vanishing remainder is treated as $o(\ln E)$, which holds for a regular approach to the limit.

roles.why: Crossing makes $F_-$ odd and lets one dispersion relation cover both processes.
The optical theorem turns the cross-section difference into $\operatorname{Im}F_-$.
It expresses $\operatorname{Re}F_-$ through $\operatorname{Im}F_-$.
Finite limits give a number $d$, the limit of the difference.
A bounded ratio contradicts the logarithmic growth.

steps.slogan: Form the odd amplitude and its imaginary part.
steps.detail: Put $F_-=F_{ab}-F_{a\bar b}$. Crossing gives $F_-(-E)=-F_-(E)$, and the optical theorem gives $\operatorname{Im}F_-=k\Delta$ with $\Delta=\sigma_{ab}-\sigma_{a\bar b}$. Assume $\Delta\to d\neq0$.

steps.slogan: Evaluate the real part by the once-subtracted dispersion relation.
steps.detail: For the even function $G=F_-/E$, with $\operatorname{Im}G\to d$, the relation gives $\operatorname{Re}G(E)=c+\frac{2E^2}{\pi}\,\mathrm{P}\!\!\int\frac{\operatorname{Im}G(E')\,dE'}{E'(E'^2-E^2)}$. Partial fractions give $\operatorname{Re}G(E)=-\frac{2d}{\pi}\ln E+O(1)$.

steps.slogan: Compare the real part with the imaginary part.
steps.detail: Then $\operatorname{Re}F_-\sim-\frac{2d}{\pi}E\ln E$, while $\operatorname{Im}F_-\sim dE$. So the ratio $\operatorname{Re}F_-/E$ grows without bound like $\ln E$.

steps.slogan: Contradict the bounded real-to-imaginary ratio.
steps.detail: The last hypothesis says $\operatorname{Re}F_-/E$ is bounded, but step 3 shows $|\operatorname{Re}F_-/E|\to\infty$ when $d\ne0$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that the difference of the cross sections vanishes.
steps.detail: The assumption $d\neq0$ is impossible, so the limit is $d=0$. Hence $\sigma_{a\bar b}-\sigma_{ab}\to0$ as the energy grows.

concepts.c:dispersion-relation: It links the real and imaginary parts of the forward amplitude.
concepts.c:cross-section: The cross sections are the quantities compared.
concepts.c:analytic-function: Analyticity of the amplitude is what crossing and dispersion use.

source.note: The standard dispersion-theory derivation; the original statement is I. Ya. Pomeranchuk, Soviet Physics JETP 7 (1958), 499, and a textbook account is R. J. Eden, High Energy Collisions of Elementary Particles (Cambridge University Press, 1967).

statement: Let $L/K$ be a finite field extension of odd degree. If $L$ is a [Pythagorean field](c:pythagorean-field), then $K$ is a Pythagorean field.

hypotheses.text: The [extension](c:field-extension) $L/K$ is finite of odd [degree](c:degree-of-an-extension).
The field $L$ is [Pythagorean](c:pythagorean-field): every sum of two squares in $L$ is a square.

conclusion: Every sum of two squares in $K$ is a square in $K$.

proofs.name: Degree of a quadratic subextension
proofs.slogan: A nonsquare sum of two squares in $K$ would give a quadratic subfield of the odd extension $L$.
proofs.scope: The odd-degree member of the Diller-Dress family. The full Diller-Dress theorem, for finite extensions of any degree, is not proved here.

roles.why: Odd degree forbids a quadratic subextension by the tower law.
It makes the sum of two squares a square in $L$.

steps.slogan: Suppose that some sum of two squares in $K$ is not a square.
steps.detail: Take $c=a^2+b^2$ with $a,b\in K$ and $c$ not a square in $K$. We derive a contradiction.

steps.slogan: Show that $c$ is a square in $L$.
steps.detail: The element $c=a^2+b^2$ is a sum of two squares of $L$. Since $L$ is [Pythagorean](c:pythagorean-field), $c=d^2$ for some $d\in L$.

steps.slogan: Place the quadratic field $K(\sqrt c)$ inside $L$.
steps.detail: Because $c$ is not a square in $K$, the polynomial $X^2-c$ is irreducible, so $[K(\sqrt c):K]=2$. The root $d$ lies in $L$, so $K\subseteq K(\sqrt c)\subseteq L$.

steps.slogan: Use the tower law to contradict the odd degree.
steps.detail: The tower law gives $[L:K]=[L:K(\sqrt c)]\cdot2$, an even number. This contradicts the odd degree, so every such $c$ is a square in $K$.

concepts.c:field-extension: The proof studies a finite extension $L/K$ and its subfields.
concepts.c:degree-of-an-extension: The multiplicativity of degrees in the tower gives the contradiction.
concepts.c:pythagorean-field: The property is assumed for $L$ and proved for $K$.

source.note: A direct argument using the tower law; the general theorem is R. Diller and A. Dress, Zur Galoistheorie pythagoreischer Koerper, Archiv der Mathematik 16 (1965), 148-152.

statement: A general [quaternary cubic form](c:homogeneous-polynomial) over $\mathbb C$ is a sum of five cubes of linear forms, $F=\ell_1^3+\dots+\ell_5^3$. Here general means that $F$ lies in a nonempty [Zariski open](c:zariski-topology) subset of the space of cubic forms.

hypotheses.text: The ground field is $\mathbb C$.
The form $F$ is a general [cubic form](c:homogeneous-polynomial) in four variables.

proofs.name: Dimension count and apolarity
proofs.slogan: The sum-of-five-cubes map has equal source and target dimension and an invertible differential at one point, so it is dominant.
proofs.scope: Existence for general $F$ over $\mathbb C$. Uniqueness of the pentahedron (Sylvester) is not proved here.

roles.why: Characteristic $0$ and algebraic closure let ranks of differentials give dimensions.
The conclusion is claimed only on a dense open set, which dominance supplies.

steps.slogan: Define the sum-of-cubes map and count dimensions.
steps.detail: Let $\Phi(\ell_1,\dots,\ell_5)=\sum\ell_i^3$ from $(\mathbb C^4)^5$ to the space of cubic forms. Both spaces have dimension $20$.

steps.slogan: Compute the image of the differential of $\Phi$.
steps.detail: The differential at $(\ell_i)$ sends $(m_i)$ to $3\sum\ell_i^2m_i$. Its image is the span of all $\ell_i^2 m$ with $m$ linear.

steps.slogan: Describe the orthogonal complement of this span by apolarity.
steps.detail: With $\ell=p\cdot x$ one has $G(\partial)\ell^3=6G(p)$ and $G(\partial)(\ell^2m)=2\,dG_p(m)$. So $G$ is orthogonal to the span exactly when $G$ is singular at all five points $p_i$.

steps.slogan: Show that no cubic is singular at five general points.
steps.detail: Take $p_i=e_0,\dots,e_3,(1,1,1,1)$. Singularity at the $e_i$ leaves only the four monomials $x_ix_jx_k$ with distinct indices, and singularity at $(1,1,1,1)$ gives a linear system with matrix $J-I$, which has determinant $-3$. So $G=0$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that $\Phi$ is dominant.
steps.detail: The differential has rank $20$ at this point, so the image of $\Phi$ has dimension $20$. By Chevalley's theorem the image is constructible and dense, so it contains a nonempty open set.

concepts.c:homogeneous-polynomial: The objects are homogeneous cubic polynomials in four variables.
concepts.c:zariski-topology: Generality is stated by membership in a Zariski open set.

source.note: The classical apolarity argument of Sylvester's pentahedral theorem, as in Dolgachev, Classical Algebraic Geometry (Cambridge University Press, 2012), chapter 9.

statement: Let $\psi$ solve the [wave equation](c:wave-equation) on the exterior of a Schwarzschild black hole ([Schwarzschild metric](c:schwarzschild-metric)), spherically symmetric, with smooth compactly supported data. At a fixed radius $r_0>2M$, $\psi(\tau,r_0)=c\,\tau^{-3}+O(\tau^{-3-\varepsilon})$, with $c$ given by the data and nonzero for generic data.

hypotheses.text: The field $\psi$ solves $\Box_g\psi=0$ on the Schwarzschild exterior, with spherical symmetry.
The initial data are smooth and compactly supported on a hypersurface crossing the horizon.
The radius $r_0$ is fixed and larger than $2M$.

conclusion: The field decays like $\tau^{-3}$ at fixed radius.

proofs.name: Time integral and Newman-Penrose constant
proofs.slogan: Integrate the field in time to a solution with a nonzero Newman-Penrose constant, find its sharp $\tau^{-2}$ decay, and differentiate.
proofs.scope: The spherically symmetric case $\ell=0$ for the linear wave equation, an outline of the published proof; general $\ell$ gives $\tau^{-2\ell-3}$ and is not covered. The weighted energy estimates rest on the cited work.

roles.why: The wave equation gives the conservation law and the time integral.
Compact support makes the Newman-Penrose constant of $\psi$ vanish and the time integral well defined.
A fixed radius lets the decay in $\tau$ be read off the sharp asymptotics.

steps.slogan: Construct the time integral $\psi^{(1)}$ with $\partial_\tau\psi^{(1)}=\psi$.
steps.detail: Because the data have compact support, the radial ODE for the time integral can be solved. This gives a solution $\psi^{(1)}$ of the wave equation with $\partial_\tau\psi^{(1)}=\psi$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\psi^{(1)}$ has a nonzero Newman-Penrose constant.
steps.detail: The constant of $\psi$ is zero. The constant $I^{(1)}$ of $\psi^{(1)}$ is an explicit integral of the data, and it is nonzero for generic data.

steps.slogan: Prove weighted energy decay estimates for $\psi^{(1)}$.
steps.detail: The $r^p$ hierarchy of weighted energy estimates controls $\psi^{(1)}$ from the horizon to null infinity. It yields decay rates in $\tau$ for the energies of $\psi^{(1)}$.

steps.slogan: Derive the sharp $\tau^{-2}$ asymptotics of $\psi^{(1)}$ at fixed radius.
steps.detail: Using $I^{(1)}\neq0$ and the estimates of step 3, $\psi^{(1)}(\tau,r_0)=4I^{(1)}\tau^{-2}+O(\tau^{-2-\varepsilon})$ at fixed $r_0$. The asymptotics also hold after differentiation in $\tau$.

steps.slogan: Differentiate in $\tau$ to get the asymptotics of $\psi$.
steps.detail: Since $\psi=\partial_\tau\psi^{(1)}$, the differentiated asymptotics of step 4 give $\psi(\tau,r_0)=-8I^{(1)}\tau^{-3}+O(\tau^{-3-\varepsilon})$ at the fixed radius. This is the claimed law with $c=-8I^{(1)}$.

concepts.c:wave-equation: The field obeys the wave equation, which gives its conservation laws.
concepts.c:schwarzschild-metric: The geometry of the exterior sets the decay rates.

source.ref: Y. Angelopoulos, S. Aretakis and D. Gajic, Late-time asymptotics for the wave equation on spherically symmetric, stationary spacetimes, Advances in Mathematics 323 (2018), 529-621
source.note: The paper proves sharp late-time asymptotics; the law itself is due to R. H. Price, Physical Review D 5 (1972), 2419 and 2439.

statement: Let $T$ be a [closed positive current](c:closed-positive-current) of bidegree $(1,1)$ on a complex manifold $X$ and $c>0$. Then the set $E_c(T)=\{x:\nu(T,x)\ge c\}$ of points with [Lelong number](c:lelong-number) at least $c$ is an [analytic set](c:analytic-set) of $X$.

hypotheses.text: $T$ is a [closed positive current](c:closed-positive-current) of bidegree $(1,1)$ on the complex manifold $X$.
The level $c$ is a positive real number.

conclusion: The upper level set $E_c(T)$ is an analytic subset of $X$.

proofs.name: Bergman approximation of potentials
proofs.slogan: Approximate a local potential by logarithms of Bergman sums whose Lelong numbers are vanishing orders, then intersect the analytic level sets.
proofs.scope: The case of $(1,1)$ currents, which is local; Siu's theorem for all bidimensions is the cited original. The $L^2$ approximation inequality rests on the cited work.

roles.why: The current has local plurisubharmonic potentials whose Lelong numbers are those of $T$.
The level $c$ shifts by $n/m$ in the intersection step.

steps.slogan: Write $T=i\partial\bar\partial\varphi$ locally with $\varphi$ plurisubharmonic.
steps.detail: On a small ball, closedness and positivity give a plurisubharmonic $\varphi$ with $T=i\partial\bar\partial\varphi$. The [Lelong number](c:lelong-number) of $T$ at $x$ is that of $\varphi$, so $E_c(T)=E_c(\varphi)$ locally.

steps.slogan: Approximate $\varphi$ by Bergman logarithms $\varphi_m$.
steps.detail:
Let $g_{m,j}$ be an orthonormal basis of holomorphic functions with $\int|g|^2e^{-2m\varphi}<\infty$, and set $\varphi_m= rac1{2m}\log\sum_j|g_{m,j}|^2$. Hormander's $L^2$ estimates (Demailly) give $
u(\varphi)-n/m\le
u(\varphi_m)\le
u(\varphi)$ at every point.

steps.slogan: Read the Lelong numbers of $\varphi_m$ as vanishing orders.
steps.detail: For a sum of squares of holomorphic functions, $\nu(\varphi_m,x)=\frac1m\min_j\operatorname{ord}_x g_{m,j}$. So $\{\nu(\varphi_m)\ge c'\}$ is the common zero set of all derivatives of the $g_{m,j}$ up to order $mc'$.

steps.slogan: Show that each set $E_{c'}(\varphi_m)$ is analytic.
steps.detail: By step 3 it is a common zero set of holomorphic functions, hence an [analytic set](c:analytic-set).

steps.slogan: Express $E_c(\varphi)$ as an intersection of such analytic sets.
steps.detail: Step 2 gives $E_c(\varphi)\subseteq E_{c-n/m}(\varphi_m)\subseteq E_{c-n/m}(\varphi)$ for all $m$, so $E_c(\varphi)=\bigcap_mE_{c-n/m}(\varphi_m)$. An arbitrary intersection of analytic sets is analytic, because of local [Noetherianity](c:noetherian-ring) of the ring of holomorphic germs.

concepts.c:closed-positive-current: Closedness and positivity give the local plurisubharmonic potential.
concepts.c:lelong-number: The upper level sets of the Lelong number are the sets shown analytic.
concepts.c:analytic-set: Analytic sets are closed under arbitrary intersections locally.
concepts.c:noetherian-ring: Noetherianity makes an infinite intersection of analytic sets a finite one.

source.ref: Y.-T. Siu, Analyticity of sets associated to Lelong numbers and the extension of closed positive currents, Inventiones Mathematicae 27 (1974), 53-156
source.note: Siu's original proof; the Bergman approximation route is due to J.-P. Demailly (Complex Analytic and Differential Geometry, chapter III).
